sentences: Beneath a swirling night sky, a small village lies asleep.
Vincent van Gogh painted this in June 1889, and today it hangs in The Museum of Modern Art in New York.
The canvas measures 73.
7 by 92.1 centimetres.
That year he was staying at the asylum in Saint-Rémy in southern France.
He watched the pre-dawn sky from his east-facing bedroom window, but he painted the picture by day in his ground-floor studio, blending memory and imagination.
Look at the centre of the sky.
Enormous swirls coil into one another, like wind or like waves.
The texture of the thickly applied paint is still alive, so the whole surface seems to move.
Come closer and you can see each short brushstroke.
Thanks to impasto, the technique of laying paint on thickly, the direction of every stroke becomes a current of light.
Yellow, white and many shades of blue lie side by side, stroke against stroke.
At the upper right, a crescent moon glows inside a bright halo.
Records suggest the actual moon at the time was not a crescent.
Van Gogh painted the moon he carried in his mind, not the one he actually saw.
The brightest star, just to the right of the cypress, is usually identified as Venus, the morning star.
Van Gogh wrote to his brother Theo that before sunrise he saw nothing but the morning star, which looked very big.
Even the halo around the star swirls.
On the left, a cypress shoots up like a flame, linking earth to sky.
In Europe the cypress is associated with death and graveyards, but scholars disagree about whether Van Gogh meant that here.
Dark and flickering, the tree fills almost the full height of the canvas.
The village and church spire were not in his view at all.
The village is based on a sketch made from a hillside, and the spire, some think, looks more like a church from his native Netherlands than one in Provence.
Small yellow lights glow in the village windows.
Unlike the violent movement overhead, the village below is drawn with calm, orderly lines.
That contrast makes the sky heave all the more.
Van Gogh painted the view from that window, in one version or another, many times, yet he considered this one a failure.
Since it entered the museum in 1941, it has become the best-loved night sky in the world.
Step back for a moment and take in the whole canvas once again.
Between the flame-like cypress, the swirling sky and the sleeping village, where does your eye rest the longest?
